problem: Calling many-inputs-one-output regression 'multivariate regression' clashes with the usual textbook meaning, where multivariate regression means several output variables at once. The clarifying clause helps, but a student can still carry the wrong label into an exam.
fix: Say plainly: this is multiple linear regression (many inputs, one output). Note that 'multivariate' is usually reserved for models with several outputs, so it is a loose name here.

problem: 'other losses need iterative search' is too strong. Least-absolute-deviation regression is solved exactly as a linear program, not by iterative search, so the sentence can mislead.
fix: Say: squared error is the default because it gives a closed-form answer; other losses such as absolute error have no such formula and need a different solver, often an iterative one — see 2.2.

problem: The transpose is written as plain 'XTX' and 'XTy' in the running text and in the term definitions, while the displayed formula uses a proper superscript. On a phone a student can read XTX as X times T times X.
fix: Write X<sup>T</sup>X and X<sup>T</sup>y consistently everywhere: 'the normal equation X<sup>T</sup>Xw = X<sup>T</sup>y', 'X<sup>T</sup>X is a (p+1) × (p+1) matrix', 'X<sup>T</sup>y is a (p+1) × 1 vector'.
